strengths: Introduces a novel, well-motivated framework for studying Mamba's in-context learning via random Markov chains, paralleling successful analogous studies for transformers, enabling precise theoretical characterization.

Provides a rigorous theorem (Thm. 1) proving that a simplified MambaZero model can represent the Bayes/minimax-optimal Laplacian smoothing estimator for first-order Markov chains, with a full constructive proof.

Complements the achievability result with an information-theoretic lower bound (Thm. 2) showing that any recurrent model (including Mamba) needs hidden dimension/precision scaling exponentially in the Markov order to represent the optimal estimator, giving a matching characterization.
Careful ablation studies isolate convolution as the key architectural component responsible for Mamba's success on this task, which is a non-obvious and interesting empirical finding.

Extends findings beyond simple Markov chains to a switching Markov model, showing the selectivity mechanism (a_t) is used to reset state at switch points, and shows a related convolution effect on real language modeling (WikiText-103), suggesting some external validity.
Clear exposition of the Mamba architecture and problem setup, with reproducibility details (hyperparameters, architecture tables) included in the appendix.
weaknesses: The main theoretical result (Thm. 1) is proven only for first-order Markov chains (k=1); the extension to general k is left as an unproven conjecture, despite being central to the paper's broader claims of 'all Markovian orders' in the abstract.

The theoretical analysis is conducted on 'MambaZero,' a substantially simplified variant of Mamba stripped of ReLU nonlinearity and gating; while ablations justify this simplification empirically, the formal guarantees do not directly cover the full Mamba/Mamba-2 architecture used in practice.

Experiments are conducted at small scale (binary alphabet, 1-2 layer models, small hidden dimensions) and using a specific synthetic data-generating process (product-Dirichlet Markov chains); it is unclear how well these findings transfer to pretrained Mamba models or larger vocabularies/tasks.

The natural language experiment (Sec. 5.2) is limited to a single dataset (WikiText-103) with small models and reports only a single perplexity number, offering fairly thin evidence for the generality of the convolution-importance claim in realistic language modeling settings.

Comparisons to transformers are somewhat informal (based on empirical curves and a cited result about induction heads) rather than a rigorous side-by-side theoretical characterization, making the 'unlike transformers' claim in the abstract only partially substantiated.

The lower bound in Thm. 2 is for generic bounded-precision recurrent models and shows an expected exponential-in-k scaling reminiscent of known results for HMM/counting-based sequential models, somewhat limiting its novelty as a stand-alone contribution.

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored question: the theoretical ICL capabilities of Mamba, in contrast to the substantial existing literature on transformers.

The empirical finding that convolution (rather than the selective SSM recurrence, ReLU, or gating) is the key architectural driver of Mamba's ability to match the Laplacian smoothing estimator is a genuinely interesting and non-obvious mechanistic insight, and is validated with reasonably careful ablations (Fig. 3).

Theorem 1 gives an explicit, verifiable parameter construction showing that a simplified MambaZero model can represent the order-1 add-β estimator to arbitrary precision, which is a concrete theoretical contribution.

The complementary lower bound (Theorem 2) showing that any recurrent/state-space model needs hidden dimension scaling as Ω(2^k) to match the Laplacian estimator for order-k chains is a nice piece of theory that connects representational capacity to computational cost.
The switching Markov chain experiment nicely illustrates the interpretability of the selection mechanism (a_t) beyond the plain Markov setting.
weaknesses: There is a substantive tension between the abstract's claim that Mamba "efficiently learns" the optimal Laplacian estimator "for all Markovian orders" and Theorem 2, which shows that any recurrent model (including Mamba) needs hidden dimension exponential in the order k to achieve this — the paper does not adequately reconcile or qualify this apparent contradiction, giving the impression of overclaiming in the abstract/intro.

The central representational result (Theorem 1) is proven only for the first-order case (k=1); the general-order claim is left as an unproven conjecture (Conjecture 1), despite the title and abstract suggesting a general, resolved theory ("for all Markovian orders").

The theoretical construction is for a heavily simplified "MambaZero" variant (no ReLU, no gating, L1 normalization instead of softmax, very specific hand-picked parameter values satisfying ad hoc algebraic constraints) rather than the actual Mamba/Mamba-2 architecture used empirically; the gap between this idealized construction and the trained model is not tightly bridged, and the result is a representability existence proof, not a proof that gradient-based training actually converges to this solution.

The empirical study is restricted to a binary alphabet, small model/state dimensions, and short training runs; the natural-language experiment (Sec. 5.2) uses only one dataset, one sequence length, and reports fairly small, possibly confounded perplexity differences (e.g., convolution also mildly helps the Transformer), which is thin evidence for the generality claim.

Baseline comparisons with Transformers appear somewhat informal ("we report the best performance for all these models" without detailed hyperparameter/architecture matching disclosure in the main text), making the qualitative comparison between single/two-layer Transformers and single-layer Mamba less rigorous than warranted for a strong claim of Mamba's superiority.

The overall methodological approach (studying ICL via random Markov chains and connecting it to Bayes-optimal/minimax estimators) closely follows an existing line of work on transformers (Nichani et al., Rajaraman et al., Edelman et al., Makkuva et al.), so the conceptual novelty is primarily in porting this framework to Mamba rather than introducing fundamentally new analysis tools.

The proof of Theorem 2 relies on strong assumptions (product-Dirichlet prior, ergodicity/mixing arguments invoked somewhat informally) and the extension claims to KL-divergence-based guarantees and general alphabets are left as unproven remarks rather than formal results.

strengths: Provides the first rigorous theoretical connection between Mamba and an optimal statistical estimator (Laplacian/add-β smoothing), filling a genuine gap in understanding SSM learning mechanisms.

Strong combination of theory and experiment: Theorem 1 gives an explicit constructive proof that a simplified MambaZero can approximate the Bayes-optimal estimator for first-order Markov chains, and Theorem 2 provides a matching information-theoretic lower bound showing exponential dependence on Markov order for any recurrent architecture with bounded precision/dimension.

Careful ablation studies isolate convolution as the crucial architectural component enabling in-context Markov estimation, and this finding is validated not only on the synthetic Markov task but also (to a lesser degree) on real language modeling with WikiText-103.

Interesting comparison with transformers showing single-layer Mamba matches a 2-layer transformer (and beats a 1-layer transformer), consistent with known induction-head literature on transformer depth requirements, adding external validity to the claims.

The extension to the switching Markov process (non-Markovian data) is a nice additional experiment showing the selectivity gate a_t is used exactly to reset counts when needed, giving further mechanistic insight beyond the Laplacian smoothing result.
The paper is clearly written, well organized, with proofs deferred to appendices, and the intuition sections (e.g., proof sketch, role of convolution window w ≥ k+1) are explained accessibly.
weaknesses: The main theorem (Thm. 1) is proven rigorously only for first-order Markov chains (k=1); the higher-order case is left as an empirically-supported conjecture, weakening the completeness of the theoretical contribution.

The theoretical analysis relies on a substantially simplified 'MambaZero' architecture that removes ReLU nonlinearities and gating; although ablations suggest this preserves empirical performance, it remains a nontrivial abstraction from the full Mamba/Mamba-2 model that is actually deployed in practice.

The construction in the proof of Theorem 1 is highly specific/hand-crafted (exact parameter choices satisfying particular algebraic conditions), and while it demonstrates representational capacity, it does not establish that gradient descent actually converges to this or an equivalent solution—this is only supported by fitting the general qualitative pattern in empirical observations (e.g., a_t ≈ 1) rather than a full optimization/learnability analysis.
Theory is restricted to a binary vocabulary X = {0,1}; while the authors state generalization to larger alphabets is straightforward, this is not formally shown.

The natural language modeling experiment (Sec 5.2) shows a fairly small model scale (~14M params, 2-4 layers) and the perplexity improvement from convolution for the Transformer baseline is marginal but still present (29.28 → 28.67), somewhat muddying the claimed contrast between Mamba and Transformer reliance on convolution.

The paper's comparisons are limited to shallow (1-2 layer) transformers/Mamba variants; it is unclear how the theoretical picture and Laplacian-smoothing behavior generalize to deeper, more realistic model stacks, which the authors acknowledge as future work.

strengths: Novel and clearly motivated question: characterizing Mamba's ICL capabilities via the Markov-ICL framework, filling a gap since most prior Mamba ICL work is empirical.

Strong theory-empirics alignment: the paper backs its theoretical construction (Theorem 1, MambaZero) with careful empirical verification of the intermediate claims (e.g., a_t≈1, orthogonality of count vectors, convergence of the count-independent term to β), which is a nice methodological practice that makes the proof sketch credible rather than just a black-box existence result.

The identification of convolution (rather than gating/non-linearity) as the key architectural ingredient is an interesting and actionable insight, and is validated across several settings (varying state space size, depth, over-parametrization, hold-out generalization, and even natural language perplexity experiments on WikiText-103).

Provides both a constructive upper bound (Thm 1, extended with a dimension-reduction result Thm 4) and an information-theoretic lower bound (Thm 2, Ω(2^k) hidden dimension) for representing the Laplacian estimator, giving a fairly complete picture of representational power for first-order and higher-order chains.
Extension beyond Markov chains (switching Markov process) nicely demonstrates the functional role of the selectivity gate a_t, adding conceptual depth beyond the main first-order result.
Extensive experimental details, ablations, and hyperparameter documentation (appendices E, F) support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The main positive theoretical result (Theorem 1) is proved for a substantially simplified model (MambaZero, without ReLU nonlinearity, gating, or MLP, and with L1 normalization instead of softmax), which departs materially from the true Mamba/Mamba-2 architecture used in the empirical study; this gap between the theory's object and the practical architecture weakens the paper's central claim of "how Mamba represents" the estimator.

The construction is existential (there exists a parameter setting achieving zero KL), not a learnability/convergence result; the paper explicitly defers analysis of gradient-based learning dynamics to future work, which somewhat limits the claim that Mamba "learns" the estimator (as opposed to being merely capable of representing it).

The higher-order Markov case is only supported empirically (Fig. 1b) without a matching constructive upper bound analogous to Theorem 1, leaving an asymmetry between the tight first-order theory and the more speculative higher-order claims.

The comparison to transformers is explicitly de-emphasized by the authors but is scattered and somewhat inconsistent (e.g., 1-layer Mamba tracks the optimal estimator better empirically for order 1, yet the lower bound suggests Mamba is exponentially worse than transformers in k), and this tension is not deeply analyzed.

Experiments are conducted on small synthetic models and a relatively small-scale language modeling benchmark (WikiText-103, ~14-110M parameters); it is unclear how well the convolution-centric insights transfer to larger, more realistic Mamba deployments or more complex data distributions.

The Dirichlet-prior data-generating assumption (i.i.d. per-context kernels from Dir(β·1)) is a fairly stylized setting; robustness of the conclusions to different priors or non-Dirichlet Markov structures is not explored, limiting generality claims.

strengths: Extends the Markov-ICL analysis framework (previously used for transformers, e.g. Edelman et al. 2024) to Mamba/SSMs for the first time, filling a genuine gap in the literature.

The main theorem (Thm. 1) gives an explicit, constructive parameterization showing that a simplified Mamba variant (MambaZero) can exactly represent the Bayes/minimax-optimal Laplacian smoothing estimator for first-order Markov chains, with a nice dimension-reduction result for the binary case (Thm. 4).

The complementary lower bound (Thm. 2), showing that recurrent architectures need hidden dimension scaling as Ω(2^k) to represent the k-th order estimator, is a nice fundamental-limits result and is empirically corroborated (Fig. 6).

Broad and fairly systematic empirical validation: multiple state sizes, model depths, over-parameterized regimes, hold-out experiments, comparisons with transformers/linear attention, a non-Markovian 'switching' process, and real language-modeling experiments (WikiText-103, PG-19) with matched parameter counts.

Clear ablations isolating the role of convolution (and later gating) as the key architectural ingredient, with the identified mechanism (state decay a_t≈1, window ≥ k+1, orthogonality of count-related vectors) empirically verified and directly tied to the theoretical construction.
Well-organized presentation connecting theory and experiments; proofs are given in detail in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core theoretical result is an existence/constructive proof for a hand-simplified 'MambaZero' model tailored so that its recurrence can be unrolled into transition counts; it does not establish that gradient-descent training actually converges to this construction, only that a matching construction exists — the link between representability and learnability rests entirely on empirical observation rather than proof.

The formal representation theorem (Thm. 1) is restricted to first-order Markov chains; the claimed generalization to higher orders (a central selling point of the abstract/title) is only supported empirically (Fig. 1b, Fig. 3b) and not proven, leaving a substantial gap between the theoretical and empirical claims.

The 'fundamental role of convolution' framing is somewhat oversold given the paper's own findings: Table 5 shows the relative importance of convolution shrinks substantially in deeper, more realistic language models, and gating is shown to matter comparably or more (Table 4) in the NLP setting, complicating the paper's headline mechanistic story.

Experiments remain largely on small-scale, synthetic, low-alphabet-size Markov tasks and small language models (14M–200M parameters); the leap to 'even outside the realm of Markovian data' and to practical language modeling is thin (a single perplexity table with modest gains, no scaling trend analysis, limited seeds/statistics).

The Mamba vs. Transformer comparison is inconsistently treated — the paper alternates between claiming this is not its focus and drawing comparative conclusions (e.g., 1-layer Mamba matches optimality while 1-layer Transformer does not, but Transformers need only linear-in-k dimension vs. exponential for Mamba) — this creates an unclear narrative about what is actually being claimed as Mamba's distinguishing advantage.

Statistical rigor of empirical claims is modest: most plots use only 5 repetitions with fairly wide error bands, and key mechanistic claims (e.g., near-orthogonality of count vectors, a_t≈1) are supported by single illustrative runs (Fig. 4, 5) rather than systematic statistics across settings.

Overall novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely transplants an existing analysis paradigm and add-β/Laplacian-smoothing connection (well established for transformers and classical universal prediction) onto a new architecture, with the technical contribution being a careful but not conceptually novel matching of Mamba's specific equations to known counting estimators.

strengths: First rigorous theoretical connection between Mamba's representational capacity and a classical optimal statistical estimator (Laplacian/add-β smoothing), filling an important gap given the largely empirical prior literature on Mamba's ICL abilities.

The constructive proof for Theorem 1 (and the dimension-reduced Theorem 4) is detailed and explicit, and importantly its structure closely mirrors what is empirically observed in trained models (near-unity state-transition factor, orthogonal count-related inner products, convergence of count-independent term to β), lending credibility that the theory explains the actual learned mechanism rather than being a disconnected existence proof.
The complementary lower bound (Theorem 2) showing exponential-in-k dimension requirements for any recurrent architecture is a nice fundamental-limits result and is empirically corroborated (Fig. 6).

Extensive and careful ablation studies isolate convolution as the key architectural component (more so than gating/nonlinearity) for the Markov task, with control experiments removing/adding convolution to both Mamba and Transformers.

Good robustness checks: multiple state sizes, deeper networks, over-parameterized settings, hold-out/generalization experiments, and a non-Markovian switching-chain experiment showing how the selectivity gate at is used for change-point detection.

Findings are shown to partially generalize beyond the synthetic Markov setting to real language modeling (WikiText-103, and further to PG-19 with deeper models in the appendix), strengthening the practical relevance of the convolution-importance claim.

Clear exposition, well-organized transition from empirical phenomenon to theoretical explanation to broader validation, with reproducible experimental details (hyperparameter tables) and code availability.
weaknesses: The main representation-power theorem is restricted to first-order Markov chains; higher-order results are only empirical (Fig. 1b, Fig. 3b), so the theoretical story is incomplete for the general k-th order case despite being the paper's central motivating setting.

The paper explicitly sidesteps learning dynamics (why/how gradient descent converges to the constructed solution), which is arguably the more interesting and harder question; the current contribution characterizes representational capacity/existence rather than learnability guarantees.

The Mamba-vs-Transformer comparisons, while informative, are somewhat secondary and not fully controlled (e.g., different known bounds - exponential in k for Mamba vs linear in k for 3-layer transformers - are drawn from different papers/analyses rather than a unified comparison), which limits how strongly the 'Mamba vs Transformer' claims can be interpreted.

The theoretical framework relies heavily on the specific Dirichlet-prior/product-Dirichlet assumption for optimality of Laplacian smoothing; it's unclear how sensitive the results are to deviations from this idealized generative assumption, and this is not discussed as a limitation.

Natural language experiments use relatively small-scale models (14M–200M parameters) and only two datasets, limiting the strength of claims about generality to realistic large-scale language modeling; perplexity gaps from convolution ablation shrink substantially with more layers, suggesting the single-layer insight may not transfer straightforwardly to deep, practical models.

MambaZero, the model used for the formal representation-capacity proof, is a simplified variant of full Mamba (removing ReLU, gating, MLP); while ablations support that this simplification preserves task-relevant behavior in the synthetic setting, the gap between MambaZero and full production Mamba/Mamba-2 is not rigorously bounded.
